en: He was especially resentful toward them.
Ismayyl's Kishimjan—
She was a skilled woman,
She was Ismayyl's daughter.
When Kanykey came on her journey to Bukhara,
When she handed over Semetey,
At his nursing-infant age,
She carried him about and raised him,
She was particularly close to him from the start.
Semetey, lord of Bukhara,
That daughter of yours who came,
Was the elder sister Semetey loved as his own life.
Walking up, weeping in distress,
Where she saw the boy,
Pleading as no other mortal did:
“One who would not tire if ridden six months,
My dear Semetey—
My black winged steed, my swift horse,
Moreover, my sibling of the same nest,
My kin, born of the same seed.
My black-blazed hawk,
The one I open my mouth to kiss,
The one I open my eyes to see,
My protecting presence behind me.
Oh, Semetey, my sibling,
Great khan of the fortified city,
Is it right to lie here all day?
Is it fitting for a khan to sulk?
What is this, younger brother, what is this?” she said.
A fattened lamb, sliced horse-neck fat,
Bringing food prepared,
Red raisins and dried grapes,
Liquor and food served with honor,
The lively, impetuous, dauntless woman,
With all kinds of riches mingled,
Heaping sugar like snow,
Filling her tablecloth,
Pressing the boy with pleas,
Calling him ‘sibling,’ she reached out.
The troublesome bitch prepared herself.
“The very image of a king—
My dear sibling,
Is it right to lie like a child?
Father of the people,
Collar of the armored robe,
The shooting bone among many knucklebones,
The winged steed among beasts,
The falcon among winged creatures,
The lion among the fanged,
My honored younger brother Semetey,
Is it right for him to sulk?
Food is a sweet meal—
Can a person take offense at it?
Rise, younger brother, rise,” she said.
“Rise and eat,” she said.
“Do not stay offended so long,” she said.
“I have come making bold.
May I take your troubles upon myself.
Do not lift me up and cast me into misery,” she said.
That bitch who had grown up his companion
Put her arm around his neck,
The orphan touched by Kydyr,
She began to tickle him.
The boy began to rage.
His elder sister doing this,
The outstanding hero's offspring,
His anger came and would not stop,
Without speaking foully or swearing:
“You are misfortune itself!
You have no firmly braced waist,
No place where you have girded yourself,
Led in a string of six gelded camels,
You have no camel that came for hire.
You shameless bitch,
You have no bridegroom to take you.
You have no waist to gird,
No husband to marry.
You have no grounds for mockery.
If you look and make sport,
You have no bridegroom who has come to take you.”
Speaking thus, Semetey,
The wretched orphan who sat glowering,
His elder sister Kishimjan,
Struck her squarely on the cheek.
Not wishing to kiss the bitch,
He shoved her hard away!
Sixty buttons, forty coral beads,
Struck hard by the wrestler's hand,
Shattered into fragments.
Kishimjan, light as a feather,
Went flying with a clatter.
Her precious life hard pressed,
When she braced against the dark earth,
The muscle of both palms
Was utterly torn apart.
Her two eyes becoming fire,
Kishimjan blazed!
Her anger rising beyond measure,
Kishimjan began to curse:
“Why not put a scarf upon my head,
Release me from my betrothal,
You accursed wretched orphan,
And take me in marriage?
A fool whose heart is elsewhere,
Is hard to stitch to oneself.
An enemy all the more estranged,
Is very hard to manage!
Though you rear a donkey for six years,
It will not become a swift steed, will it?
A Kyrgyz is ever someone apart,
He will not become kin, will he?
Into Temir Khan's city,
You wandered and grew up.
To Khan Ismayyl's city,
You came seeking support and grew mighty.
Offspring of a different stock,
Called my kinsman, he proves a stranger.
One raised differently cannot be stitched to you,
One whose heart differs cannot be managed!
His mother is Kanykey.
As a wife she disrupted the people.
When his mother was a girl,
She shook the world and disrupted the people.
You have turned your heart to strangers.
Go find, orphaned slave,
Your Kyrgyz people in Talas.
You have turned your heart to strangers.
Not hearing my words when I pleaded,
You have so robbed me of composure.
Go find your Kyrgyz people!”
Speaking these words thus,
Kishimjan cursed him.
Hearing the words from Kishimjan,
Again that he was Manas's,
The boy heard firmly, without doubt.
The ruler of that city,
Again came beside him,
The one they called Koloy.
He was a rash hero,
Clumsy in his thinking.
He too came up blustering,
Angry with the boy,
Again he came thundering.
He missed him when he did not see him,
He loved the boy.
Moreover, he was a close confidant,
He valued him like his faith.
Then Koloy Khan said:
“An enemy to fight, mischief,
You have come to long for,
Raiding horses from afar,
Great slaughter and pursuit.
‘No one will stand by me,’ you think,
And you have taken offense.
Do not sulk, orphan; rise up.
Come and hear what I say!
Is there a gray, hilly mountain?
My child, is there an enemy to meet at an appointed time?
Is there a firmly lodged, costly claim?
My valiant younger brother, rise up.
Is there an enemy come from Mecca?
You have lain down in distress.
Is there a shot that struck without breaking?
Spread firmly against you in front,
Is there a net of iron rope?
To fight without giving way,
Is there misery to trample and wade through?
If there is an enemy come from Beijing,
My valiant younger brother, tell me.
I shall drive them back as far as Beijing.
Amid great slaughter,
Give me Aktulpar to ride.
Tying my life to a single hair,
As a sacrifice before you,
Let my wretched soul go in!”
The hero Koloy dismounted.
Of the fine distilled liquor,
A handled cup with a golden rim,
He now filled to the brim.
Lifting the boy's head,
Your Koloy now held it out.
“My reed and mint in the water,
My Sultan Semey, my only one.
To rest in your shade,
My sheltering shrine in the depths,
If you will not drink what I offer,
My dear foal,
My hope will break.
Do not break my hope.
My plane tree, my child, rise up.
I heard news from those who came.
For twelve days you have sulked,
I heard you have taken no food.
One who does not eat will die.
One who sulks will suffer calamity.
Your guts will burn and grow diseased,
Your liver-flesh will fill with blood.
If you fall ill, boy, you will fare badly.
If precious life departs, it is a grievous matter.
You will certainly not survive.
Liquor is a bitter food.
If it is a fault, forgive me.
This precious head bows before you!
Placed before us, you bring good fortune.
I shall rely on you from Bukhara,
As though driving a countless host.
Do not sulk like a young child.
Drink this, little mischief-maker!
Walking behind, you bring good fortune.
Your towering shelter is like a countless host.
I have offered my head to you.
Drink this, little mischief-maker!”
Speaking thus, Koloy Khan,
Though he offered his head, the boy did not yield.
Koloy Khan pleaded much.
Semetey did not stir once.
Anger coming upon him, he stiffened.
He was a rash man,
Quarreling with Semetey:
“My child, have they plundered your precious goods?
Have the people of Bukhara gone, my foal,
And the Kyrgyz in Talas,
Have they slaughtered them all?
Have the people of Bukhara
Done you so great a wrong?
Why have you spoiled your disposition?
There is not the least sign of anyone slaughtering
Your Kyrgyz people in Keng-Kol.
Pouting in resentment,
No one has destroyed your court.
Bukhara is not the land of Keng-Kol.
In Talas, slashing her fat rump,
Your mother Kanykey,
They plundered her utterly and drove her away.
I am not Abyke or Kobosh.
You have grieved me with your bitter sulking.
Your migrating camp has not been wrecked from Keng-Kol.
You grieve me with your sulking.
There is no vengeance for your father, Khan Manas.
The son of a courageous lion,
‘I shall keep him as my offspring,’ he says,
That one who has been raising him—
Temir Khan has no sense!
To plunder the precious goods,
This orphan whose heart is elsewhere
Has taken such deep offense!
To wreak havoc in Bukhara.
Instead of liquor, drink stones.
If that is too little for your fancy,
Drink your father Manas's blood with it!”
Speaking thus, Koloy Khan
Began with troublesome words.
Angered, the irascible man
Dropped the boy's head upon the ground.
